extracted.intended_audience: astronomers, mathematicians, and physicists studying celestial mechanics (tides, lunar/solar forces, cometary orbits, precession)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and physical principles for (a) inferring lunar and solar tidal forces from tide observations and using those to deduce lunar density/mass and tidal effects on Earth, (b) computing precession from solar/lunar torques and Earth's mass distribution, and (c) analysing cometary motion (parallax, distance, brightness, and orbit construction using parabolic/conic fits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine lunar-to-solar tidal force ratio from tide observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer the proportion of the Moon's force to the Sun's from the proportions of tidal motions produced by those bodies — specifically by comparing tidal amplitudes at syzygy (conjunction/opposition) and at quadrature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured tidal heights at syzygies and quadratures (examples: Avon near Bristol: syzygy ≈ 45 feet, quadrature ≈ 25 feet). Model the tidal action so that in quadratures the lunar effective force is reduced by the square of the sine of the complement of the declination (numerical factor given as 841/1000 when sinus ≈ 91706/100000). Set up algebraic relations between L + S (syzygy sum) and (841/1000 L - S) (quadrature difference) to solve for L:S. Newton shows two observational data sets (Avon and Plymouth) leading to estimates ~5.46:1 and ~7.2:1 and adopts a median ≈ 6 1/3 : 1 until better observations are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert relative tidal-force ratio to absolute lunar force relative to gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the Sun's tidal force relative to terrestrial gravity, compute the Moon's tidal force relative to gravity using the previously derived L:S ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With Solar tidal force = 1 / 12,868,200 of gravity (as taken earlier), and using a median L:S ratio of 6 1/3 : 1, obtain lunar tidal force ≈ 1 / 2,031,821 of gravity. (Newton gives this explicit computation and uses it in subsequent considerations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare predicted tidal forcing to observed amplitudes, accounting for basin geometry and resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the computed tidal force is sufficient to explain observed sea-level changes, taking into account ocean width, depth, and geometric amplification in straits, bays, and shallow/long inlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect open oceans with wide east–west extent (e.g., Pacific, Atlantic) to show tidal rises of order 6, 9, 12, or 15 feet; larger seas (wider and deeper) tend to show larger tides. Narrow, shallow seas and long channels (Magellan, English Channel around England) or places where water must rush into/evacuate basins (Plymouth, Chepstow, St. Michael's/Auranches, Cambaya, Pegu) amplify tides, sometimes to tens of feet. Thus match the computed forcing to observed heights by considering whether the basin allows simultaneous rise on both sides, resonance, and flow impediments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize detectability limits of lunar tidal force in terrestrial experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The lunar tidal force magnitude is too small to be measured by pendulum experiments or ordinary static/hydrostatic experiments on Earth; its observable effect is essentially the tides of the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With lunar tidal force ≈ 1/2,031,821 of gravity, Newton argues that such small accelerations are negligible in laboratory/pendulum/hydrostatic settings; they produce a sensible effect only in the sea (the free-fluid response).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer lunar density and mass from tidal-force ratios and apparent diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the proportionality between tidal forces and the product of apparent cube of diameter and density (i.e., force ∝ density × apparent_diameter^3 combined appropriately) to deduce relative densities and masses of Moon, Sun, and Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton uses the derived L:S ratio (≈ 6 1/3 : 1) and apparent mean diameters of Sun and Moon (given as 31'27" and 32'12") together with the previously deduced density ratio of Sun:Earth (100:387) to compute Moon:Earth density ≈ 9:5 (approx.), giving Moon mass ≈ 1/26 of Earth's and surface gravity on Moon roughly half that of Earth. He states the arithmetic explicitly and uses it to conclude that the Moon is relatively dense and 'more terrestrial' than previously thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain synchronous rotation (same lunar face towards Earth) via tidal deformation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Moon were fluid, Earth's tidal action would produce an elongated figure whose major axis passes through Earth's center; that figure would naturally orient the same face toward Earth and small oscillations would return toward that equilibrium slowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton argues that the equilibrium spheroidal figure induced by Earth's attraction would make one lunar hemisphere permanently directed toward Earth; any displacement would oscillate back but very slowly because the disturbing forces are small. This furnishes a mechanistic explanation for the Moon's synchronous rotation (tidal locking) if the body started or spent time in a fluid state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute torque/efficacy from mass elements vs equatorial ring (Lemma I)
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing the total effect of particles of the Earth's exterior shell in producing a circular motion (torque) about an axis, compare the efficacy of the whole exterior shell with that of the equatorial ring: the whole exterior shell's effect is four times smaller than the equatorial ring of equal mass arranged as an annulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma I lays out the geometric decomposition (particles in a spherical cap vs equatorial ring) and shows that the total efficacy of exterior particles to drive rotation about an axis is quadruple smaller than the same mass concentrated in an equatorial annulus; this factor is used to relate local particle contributions (proportional to distance from plane QR) to aggregate torques on equinoctial points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate rotational motions of sphere and annulus by mass and geometry (Lemma II)
rubrics_metrics.description: The composite rotation of the whole Earth about an axis, as composed from motions of its constituent parts, is related to the annulus motion by a ratio depending on the mass ratio and geometric factors (moments of inertia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma II shows that the motion of a cylinder (or annulus) compared to the motion of the inscribed sphere depends on the ratio of their masses and on factors derived from the squares of radii/circumferences. Newton writes the precise composite ratio in terms of the matter ratio and numerical factors (e.g., numbers like 925275 and 1000000 arising from geometric relations). Use these moment-of-inertia comparisons to deduce how much an outer annulus will move relative to the inner globe when torqued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equinoctial point motion independent of rigidity of annulus (Lemma III)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an annulus (representing Earth's outer parts) revolves about the Sun yearly and about its axis daily with axial tilt equal to the obliquity, then the motion of the equinoctial points produced is the same whether the annulus is fluid or rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma justifies modeling Earth's outer deformable portions as an annulus for computing the equinoctial regression: the resulting motion of equinoxes depends on mass distribution and geometry, not on whether material is fluid or rigid, provided the annulus shares the same gross motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute precession of the equinoxes from solar and lunar torques (Prop. XXXIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive annual regression of equinoctial points by modeling torques due to the Sun and Moon on Earth's equatorial bulge/annulus, accounting for nodal motion of the Moon, mass distribution of Earth, and inclination effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton starts from lunar nodal motion rates and uses the annulus model (with mass proportion equal to Earth's exterior above a specified sphere) to compute reduction factors (Lemma I & II) and obtains a precession rate ~54"29' reduced to ~49"58' when adjusting for obliquity (sin complement factor ≈ 91706/100000). Adding the lunar contribution (proportional to the derived lunar tidal force) yields a combined precession close to observed ~50" per year. He further shows how assumed density distributions (altitude of material under equator) alter the computed precession and recommends intermediate density models to match observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diurnal and annual parallaxes and apparent motion anomalies to place comets among planets (Lemma IV and related text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether comets lie beyond the Moon and in planetary regions by analysing diurnal parallax, annual parallax effects, and apparent velocity variations (including retrograde/accelerations) as Earth and comet move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton explains that diurnal parallax excludes sublunary distances; annual-parallax-based arguments and the pattern of apparent acceleration/retardation (depending on whether Earth moves with or against the comet's apparent motion) permit inferring relative distances. He gives a geometric construction (points QA, QB, QC, QF; construction of g correspondences) for estimating a comet's distance from such longitudinal observations, and remarks that comets often lie below (i.e., interior to) Jupiter's orbit in perihelia and commonly approach near the Sun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate comet distance from brightness and apparent diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measured apparent diameter of the comet's coma and nucleus and the observed brightness (relative to known planets) to estimate the comet's distance: brightness falls with increasing distance both by inverse-square of illumination and by diminution of apparent diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton notes that illuminated body's brightness seen from Earth diminishes roughly in the quadruple ratio of distance due to both increased distance to Sun and reduced apparent diameter; he compares measured micrometer diameters (examples: comet 1682 capillitium 2'0" by Flamsteed; nucleus 11–12" or 10–12" fractionally) to planetary diameters (Saturn ~30" used as reference) to argue that many observed bright comets must be within Saturn's region or interior. He stresses corrections for obscuring 'smoke' (coma) vs nucleus, and uses examples from Hevelius and Flamsteed to justify proximity estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret coma and tail illumination and implications for comet proximity and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason from the light of comets' heads and tails (reflected or emitted) about the comet's proximity to the Sun and their atmospheric character: tails/heads produced by reflected solar light and scattering from coma imply closeness to Sun and an extended atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton provides corollaries: 1) Comet light is reflected solar light, 2) the frequency of comet apparitions near the Sun is explained because illuminated features are brighter when Sunward, 3) the existence of bright persistent heads and tails implies comets possess extensive atmospheres (not mere meteors) and that interplanetary resistance is negligible since cometary paths are freely traversed and often cross planetary orbits without rapid decay. He discusses alternative hypotheses (smoke vs caput emission) and their effects on distance inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comet orbits are conic sections and obey equal-areas-in-equal-times
rubrics_metrics.description: Comets move in conic sections (parabolas, ellipses, hyperbolas) with the Sun at the focus and sweep areas proportional to time (Keplerian area law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prop. XL states that comets move in conic sections whose radii to the Sun describe areas proportional to the time. Corollaries: 1) returning comets have elliptical orbits and orbital periods scale as the 3/2 power of the major axis (period ∝ a^(3/2)); 2) comet orbits with very large axes approximate parabolas closely; 3) the instantaneous speed of a comet at a given solar distance relates to the speed of a planet in a circular orbit at that distance by a factor involving the square root of distance (Newton gives explicit numerical recipe using a chosen unit semidiameter e.g., 100000000 and resulting speed factors). Use these laws to relate orbital period, axis size, and instantaneous velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a parabola through given points via finite differences (Lemma V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence of points with ordinates AH, BI, CK, ... dropped to a common baseline, obtain the parabolic curve through them by computing successive finite differences and forming a series RS = a + b p + c q + d r + ... (with adjustments for equal or unequal abscissa spacing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case 1 (equal abscissas): form successive first differences b, second differences c, third differences d, etc., scaled by 1, 1/2, 1/3, ... to build coefficients; choose an origin S and compute RS by adding terms a + b p + c q + ... where p, q, r are 1/2p, 1/3q, etc., with signs for terms on either side of S. Case 2 (unequal abscissas): divide differences by the corresponding abscissa intervals and proceed similarly. Newton notes that areas under curves (quadratures) can be approximated from the parabola and that parabolic methods allow practical quadrature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolate comet position/time by parabolic curve fitting from observations (Lemma VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence of observed longitudes (and latitudes) at known observation intervals, fit a regular curve through these points (parabola via Lemma V) to find the comet's longitude/latitude at any intermediate time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label observed times HI, IK, KL, LM and corresponding observed longitudes HA, IB, KC, LD, ME. Fit a regular curve ABCDE through these points and find its ordinate RS at the desired intermediate time HS. Newton recommends using five observations if the observed longitudinal differences are large (~10–20 degrees); if differences are small (~4–5 degrees) three or four observations suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a line through a point with prescribed intercept ratio on two given lines (Lemma VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a given point P, draw a line BC intersecting two given lines AB and AC so that the segments PB and PC have a specified ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: from P draw any PD to one of the lines, extend to E on the second line with PE:PD in the given ratio, draw EC parallel to AD; then CP:PB = PE:PD. This is a construction lemma used in subsequent geometric constructions for orbit/time relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate chord segmentation of parabola to time proportionality for small arcs (Lemma VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabola with axis through S and chord AC bisected at I, a point E where a certain constructed line meets AC cuts off a segment AE that is approximately proportional to the time required to traverse arc AC by the comet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton uses geometric area arguments: area-based proportionality of arc-subtended areas to times (area law) and constructions (take a point O with mu O = 1/2 mu I, draw OS, extend to xi so that Sxi = 2*SO, draw xi B meeting AC at E) to show AE:AC ≈ time(arc AB):time(arc AC). This lemma supports time parametrisation of parabolic arcs by chord segments and is used in interpolation algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tangential/area approximations to equate arc lengths under specific velocity models (Lemmas IX–X)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ approximations comparing arc-lengths, tangential segments, and areas to relate the distance a comet would traverse with the instantaneous velocity (e.g., compare arc AC to the length the comet would traverse if it kept tangent velocity equal to that at a given altitude SP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma IX establishes relations among certain constructed rectilinear segments and the parabola's parameter 4Smu (latus rectum). Lemma X shows that if a comet at a point mu proceeded uniformly with the velocity it has at an altitude equal to SP, in the same time it would traverse a length equal to the chord AC; Newton uses area arguments and ratios of SN:SM etc. to equate these quantities. These lemmas justify using tangent approximations and area comparisons to get short-time predictions of position from instantaneous velocity.
